title: USENIX Security '26 - United We Defend: Collaborative Membership Inference Defenses in Federated Le…

segments.text: Hello everyone. I'm Lei from the Hong
Kong Polytenic University. Today I'll
present our work united we defend
collaborative membership inference
defenses in federated learning. Next,
let me briefly introduce membership
inference attacks. The goal is to
determine whether a given query example
was included in a client's training
data. In federated learning, multiple
clients train their local models on
private data and send model updates to
the server for aggregation. Although the
raw training data never leaves the
clients, the shared models can still
reveal membership information. As
illustrated here, an attacker can
exploit either the local model of a
target client or the aggregated global
model. Given a query example, such as an
image, an audio sample, or a medical
record, the attacker analyzes a model's
behavior and predicts whether this
example is a member or a non-member of
the client's training data. So,
membership inference creates a direct
privacy risk for federated learning.
Before introducing our defense, let's
first look at how existing defenses
work. Most existing methods are built on
two common assumptions. The first
assumption is defend everyone. They
typically assume that all clients deploy
the same defense mechanism. However, in
practice, privacy requirements can vary
across clients. Some clients may need
strong protection while others may not
need protection at all. Applying defense
to every client therefore introduces
unnecessary utility loss. The second
assumption is defend alone. Each client
protects his own training data
independently without considering
collaboration with other protected
clients. This limits the opportunity to
jointly balance privacy and utility. So
existing defenses essentially provide
uniform and isolated protection. This
motivates our question. Can we defend
only the clients that need protection
and let them defend together? To address
these limitations, we rethink the basic
assumption of existing defenses. Our
idea is simple. Defense some and defend
together. First, instead of protecting
every client, we consider partial
defense where only a subset of clients
that actually need privacy protection
deploy defenses. As shown on the left,
clients two and three are protected
while the other clients continue normal
training. This avoids unnecessary
utility loss. Second, instead of
defending independently, these protected
clients form a defender coalition and
collaborate against MIAs. This
assumption is practical in real world
scenarios. For example, multiple devices
belonging to the same user may naturally
collaborate. Similarly, hospitals or
organizations under the same parent
company may share the same privacy
requirements and form a trusted
coalition. So, our goal is to provide
tailored protection through
collaboration while preserving better
model utility.
However, this new defense faces two
major limitations in federal learning.
First, the distribution of non-member
samples becomes more complex. Consider
client two in the defender coalition.
From its perspective, we now have three
types of samples. Members from client 2
itself, non-members from outside the
coalition, and non-members from outside
the coalition, and non-members from
outside federal learning. As shown on
the right, these three types can exhibit
very different loss trajectories. In
particular, samples from other defenders
may be partially exposed through
collaborative training, making their
behavior more similar to actual members.
Second, existing defenses are often
ineffective against emerging trajectory
based MIAs. These attacks do not rely on
a single model snapshot, but exploit how
sample behavior evolves throughout
training. To better understand this
problem, we further analyze the loss
trajectories of these different types of
samples. An interesting observation is
that sample exposure plays an important
role. As highlighted here, when a sample
is less exposed to the local model, its
trajectory becomes more similar to that
of other samples.
Based on this intuition, we propose our
collaborative defense coadmate. The core
idea is to reduce sample exposure to
narrow the behavioral gap between
members and non-members. To achieve this
while preserving model utility,
Kofandmid consists of three modules.
First, class guided partition
distributes different classes across the
defending clients. So each local model
is exposed to only part of the training
data. Second, because reduced exposure
may also cause utility loss, utility
aware compensation selectively brings
back high utility samples while keeping
the additional exposure limited.
Finally, aggregation neutral pertubation
further protects local updates. The
defenders add coordinated perturbations
that obscure individual behavior but
cancel each other during aggregation.
Together, these three modules reduce
sample exposure, recover model utility,
and further strengthen privacy
protection. Next, I'll explain each
model in detail.
The first model is a class guided
partition. Instead of letting every
defending client train on all of its
local classes, we partition the classes
across the coalition. As shown on the
left, different clients are assigned
different subsets of classes. Across
clients, we minimize the class overlap.
This means fewer samples are exposed to
each local model, which reduces
membership leakage. At the same time,
across a coalition, we maintain full
class coverage. So although each client
only sees part of the classes, the
coalition as a whole still covers a
complete data distribution helping
preserve model utility. So the key idea
is to assign minimally overlapping
classes, low overlap for privacy while
full coverage maintains utility.
The second module is utility aware
compensation. After the class guided
partition module, each client only
trains on its assigned classes. This
reduces sample exposure, but using only
partial training data may also cause
utility loss. To address this, we
selectively recycle samples from the
remaining classes. As shown on the left,
these unused samples are selectively
added back to each client for local
training. The recycling follows two
principles. First, we prioritize samples
with high utility contribution so that a
small number of recycle samples can
effectively recover model utility.
Second, we keep the recycling ratio low
so most samples remain unexposed to the
local model. This helps preserve the
privacy benefit from the first module.
In short, we selectively recycle samples
to recover utility with minimal privacy
cost.
The third module is aggregation neutral
pertabbation which protects the local
updates exposed to the server. The idea
is simple. Across clients, each defender
adds a perturbation to his local update.
This protects individual client behavior
and makes membership inference more
difficult. However, directly adding
pertabbations may hurt model utility. So
across the coalition, we jointly design
these perturbations to cancel out during
aggregation. For example, one client
adds delta while another adds minus
delta. In this way, the server receives
the original aggregated update while
individual local updates remain
protected. So this module achieves both
goals privacy at the client level and
utility at the coalition level. Now
let's look at the experimental results.
We compare Kofad Mid with six defense
baselines against the seven trajectory
based MIAs. Here lower attack AOC is
better and 0.5 means random guessing. In
the above blue box with a small
coalition of only two out of 10 clients,
Kofad achieves an average attack AU of
0.52 already close to random guessing
with only about 1% utility loss. In the
bottom green box, when the coalition
grows to five clients, the average AU
further drops to 0.51 while the utility
loss remains small at around 3%.
Compared with the six baselines,
Kofadomme provides consistently stronger
protection across different attacks. So
our defense achieves near random MIA
performance with comparable model
utility.
Next, we evaluate collaboration and
scalability. First, does collaboration
really help? On the left, we compare our
collaborative defense with an
independent version across different
coalition sizes. The collaborative
defense consistently achieves lower
attack AU. This shows that collaboration
improves defense effectiveness. Next, we
vary the total number of FL clients from
five to 30 on the both the pair and half
coalition settings. On the right, as the
FL system scales up, the attack AU
remains relatively stable while the
accuracy loss stays small. This
indicates that our defense remains
effective under different FL sizes. So
these results demonstrate two properties
of kofad mid collaboration provides
stronger protection and the defense
scales to different FL system sizes.
Now let's understand why kofad mid
works. First we look at the loss
trajectories on the left. After applying
our defense the three sample types show
very similar loss trajectories. This
makes them much harder for trajectory
based MIAs to distinguish. There are two
main reasons. First, less exposure. As
shown in the gray area, a large portion
of training samples are not exposed to
each local model, directly reducing the
membership signal. Second,
differentiated sample treatment.
Regarding the blue and orange areas,
most selected samples are trained
normally while small fraction receive
additional protection through our
compensation mechanism. Together,
reduced exposure and differentiated
treatment narrows the behavioral gap
between members and non-members.
Finally, we consider a stronger adaptive
attacker. So far, the attacker targets
individual local models or the global
model. But what if the attacker can
identify the defender coalition? In this
case, as shown on the left, the attacker
can aggregate the models from all
defending clients and uses coalition
level model as the new target for
membership inference. This gives the
attacker more information about the
protected clients. We evaluate this
adaptive attack on two data sets under
both small and large coalitions. As
shown in the right table, even with this
stronger attacker, Kofad Mid still
substantially reduces the attack AU in
most cases with many results remaining
close to random guessing. So even when
the coalition is exposed, our defense
remains effective against adaptive
attacks.
To wrap up, I'd like to share three key
takeaways. First, in federal learning,
not every client has the same privacy
requirement. So instead of defending
everyone, we protect only the clients
who need protection. Second, this
protected clients do not have to defend
independently. They can form a coalition
and defend together which provides
stronger protection through
collaboration.
Third, with our proposed Kofad made this
collaborative design can effectively
mitigate trajectory based membership
inference attacks while introducing only
minimal utility loss. So the main
message of this work is simple defend
some defend together and defend better.
Our paper and source code are available
here.
Thanks for your listening.
